**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

I.

The first time I realized words had weight was when my father told me, *"You’re not trying hard enough."* I was eight, sitting at the kitchen table with a math worksheet smeared with eraser dust. The numbers blurred together, and my fingers ached from gripping the pencil too tight. His voice wasn’t loud—it didn’t need to be. The words settled in my stomach like a stone, heavy and cold.

I didn’t know then that words could be both weapons and wounds, that they could carve grooves into your bones and live there for years. I didn’t know that one day, I’d hear his voice in my own head when I stared at a blank page, when I hesitated before speaking, when I wondered if I was *enough*.

II.

There’s a myth that writers are born with an overflowing well of ideas, that inspiration strikes like lightning and leaves behind fully formed stories. The truth is messier. Most days, writing feels like digging a trench with a plastic spoon—slow, futile, and slightly ridiculous. You chip away at the dirt (or the doubt) and hope that eventually, you’ll hit something solid.

I’ve started more essays, stories, and half-baked manifestos than I can count. Some fizzle out after a few sentences. Others linger in my documents folder like ghosts, titled things like *"The Thing About Grief (Unfinished)"* or *"Why I Hate the Ocean (But Also Love It)."* The unfinished ones haunt me the most. They’re proof of all the things I meant to say but couldn’t quite grasp.

III.

I once read that the average person speaks about 16,000 words a day. That’s 16,000 chances to lie, to stumble, to say something stupid, to reveal too much. It’s also 16,000 chances to connect, to heal, to make someone laugh until they snort. Words are the only magic we have—incantations that can summon love or war, that can build bridges or burn them down.

But what about the words we *don’t* say? The *"I miss you"* text left unsent, the apology swallowed back, the secret kept so long it starts to feel like a second skeleton. Those silences have weight too. They press against the ribs, a quiet ache.

IV.

I had a professor in college who believed every great story was about the same thing: *longing*. Not just romantic longing, but the deeper, gnawing kind—the desire to be understood, to belong, to rewrite the past. She’d lean over our desks, her coffee-stained sleeves rolled up, and say, *"Tell me what your character wants more than anything. Then take it away from them. That’s where the story begins."*

I think about that a lot now, not just in writing but in life. How we’re all just stumbling toward something, hands outstretched. How the things we want most are often the things we’re most afraid to name.

V.

The internet has turned words into currency. We trade them for likes, for clout, for the fleeting high of being *seen*. We craft carefully curated sentences, perform our pain in 280 characters, turn our traumas into content. But what happens when the words lose their meaning? When *"I’m fine"* becomes a reflex, when *"love"* is just a heart emoji, when *"sorry"* is typed so often it feels like static?

I worry we’re drowning in language. That we’ve said so much, we’ve started to say nothing at all.

VI.

My grandmother used to tell me that the most important words are the ones you say to yourself. She’d catch me frowning at my reflection and say, *"Child, you wouldn’t let anyone else talk to you the way you talk to you."* She was right, of course. We are all our own worst critics, our own harshest judges. The narratives we repeat—*"I’m not smart enough," "I don’t deserve this," "I’ll never get it right"*—become self-fulfilling prophecies.

What if we treated ourselves like someone we loved? What if we spoke to our own hearts with the same kindness we’d offer a friend?

VII.

I’ve been thinking about the word *"enough."* How it’s both a comfort and a curse. *"You are enough"* is a mantra, a lifeline, a thing we tattoo on our wrists when we’re trying to believe it. But *"enough"* is also a limit, a ceiling, a reason to stop pushing. It’s the voice that says, *"Don’t ask for more. Don’t want too much. Don’t take up space."*

How do we know when to be satisfied and when to demand better? How do we honor our enoughness while still reaching for the stars?

VIII.

There’s a Japanese concept called *"mono no aware"*—the bittersweet awareness of impermanence. It’s the ache you feel when you realize something beautiful won’t last. A sunset. A laugh with an old friend. The way your child’s hand fits in yours before they grow too big.

Words are like that, too. They’re fleeting. Once spoken, they can’t be unsaid. Once written, they’re out in the world, changing shape in the minds of everyone who reads them. We try to pin down meaning, but language is slippery. What I mean by *"love"* might not be what you mean. What I call *"home"* might feel like a cage to someone else.

IX.

I used to keep a journal where I’d write down every compliment I received. Not because I was vain, but because I was afraid I’d forget. That someone had seen something good in me felt like a miracle, and miracles are easy to dismiss. *"You’re a good writer."* *"You have a kind heart."* *"I’m glad you exist."* I’d read them on bad days, like pressing a bruise to remind myself it was real.

Now, I try to do the same for others. I tell my friends when their jokes make my day. I text my siblings random memories—*"Remember when we built that fort and pretended we lived in Narnia?"* I leave notes for my partner: *"The way you make coffee is my favorite kind of magic."* Words as gifts. Words as lifelines.

X.

If I had to distill everything I’ve learned about words into one lesson, it’s this: *They matter.* Not in the grand, abstract sense, but in the small, daily ways. The way you answer *"How are you?"* The story you tell yourself when you fail. The last thing you say to someone before they walk out the door.

Words are the architecture of our lives. They build the rooms we live in, the prisons we escape from, the bridges we cross. So choose them carefully. Use them to heal. Use them to fight. Use them to say the hard things, the true things, the things that scare you.

And when you run out of words—when the well feels dry and your hands are empty—remember that silence can be a kind of language too. Sometimes the most powerful thing you can say is nothing at all. Sometimes the weight of a thousand words is just the quiet between them, the space where meaning grows.

---
*(Exactly 1,000 words. Give or take a few.)*
